study.title: Acts 14 The gospel between opposition, idolatry, and perseverance
study.overview: Acts 14 shows the spread of the gospel among Jews and Gentiles, with real fruit and intense opposition. In Iconon, preaching produces faith in large numbers, but it also provokes hostility and division. In Lystra, the healing of a crippled man reveals the power of God, but almost leads the apostles to be venerated as gods; they refuse any undue honor and direct the crowd to the living God. Then the persecution worsens: Paul is stoned, he is given as dead, but he rises and continues the mission. The chapter ends with the return of missionaries to the church of Antioch, where they render account for the work of God and the opening of faith to the Gentiles.

outline.title: Preaching in Iconium and split reaction
outline.explanation: Paul and Barnabas announce the first word in the synagogue, and many Jews and Greeks believe. The resistance of the unbelieving Jews incites opposition among the Gentiles, generating division in the city and an attempt at violence that forces missionaries to flee to Lystra and Derbe. Even expelled, they do not stop preaching the gospel.

outline.title: Healing in Lystra and refusal of human worship
outline.explanation: In Lystra, Paul heals a crippled man from birth, and the crowd interprets the miracle according to his pagan religiosity, calling Barnabas and Paul by names of gods. The apostles react firmly, tear the clothes and reject sacrifices, teaching that they are only men and that the message calls all to the living God, Creator and benefactor of all things.

outline.title: stoning, perseverance and mission report
outline.explanation: Jews from other cities instigo the crowd, Paul is stoned and dragged out, but rises and resumes the journey with Barnabas. After evangelizing and strengthening disciples, they appoint elders in the churches, pass back through the cities visited and return to Antioch to report what God did, highlighting the opening of faith to the Gentiles and remaining there for a time with the disciples.

study.context: The chapter records the first missionary journey of Paul and Barnabas in regions linked to Asia Minor, including Icononius, Lystra, Derbe, Antioch and other cities in the region of Licaonia and Pamphylia. The notes show that they used to start with the synagogue and then go to other cities when they suffered opposition. It is also seen that the church of Antioch had sent them and then received them again to hear the report of the work done by God.
study.theology: Acts 14 clearly emphasizes that the Christian mission is the work of God, although carried out by human servants. Faith is born by preaching the word, not by religious manipulation. The power of God is manifested in signs and healings, but such signs are not an end in themselves; they point to the gospel and to the living God. The chapter also confronts idolatry, showing that even seemingly honorable reactions can be deeply mistaken when they attribute divine glory to men. Moreover, persecution does not invalidate the mission: on the contrary, the affliction accompanies the entry into the Kingdom of God. Finally, the chapter presents the organization of the churches through elders, prayer and fasting, indicating pastoral care and dependence on God.

scholarViews.insight: The preaching in Iconon began in the synagogue and resulted in a great response of both Jews and Greeks, but the opposition of unbelieving Jews contaminated the minds of the Gentiles against the brethren.
The healing of the crippled in Lystra illustrates human impotence for spiritual things and the need for God's grace to restore who is without force.
The crowd wanted to offer sacrifices to the apostles, but Paul and Barnabas resisted, refusing undue honors and directing the worship of the living God.

questions: Why do some people believe when the gospel is preached, while others react with hostility to the same message?
What does Paul and Barnabas' reaction in Lystra teaches about how to deal with compliments, religious fame and idolatry?
How should the claim that it is necessary to enter the Kingdom of God through many afflictions must shape the church's perseverance today?
study.practice: This chapter calls on the Christian to remain faithful when the message is received with joy and when it is rejected with violence. Concrete application is: to proclaim Christ with courage, without successfully measuring only by public acceptance; to refuse every attempt to turn servants of God into objects of veneration; and to sustain the life of the church with teaching, prayer, fasting and godly leadership. It is also appropriate to learn from Paul and Barnabas to account for everything to God and to the church, recognizing that it was the Lord who opened the door of faith.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not accurately clarify the length of stay in each city or allow to detail absolute dates of the trip. It is also not possible to safely affirm, from the notes alone, the exact identity of all the groups mentioned in ethnic or social terms beyond what the text itself and the comments indicate. Where the chapter presents reactions from the crowd, the apostolic interpretation is recorded as an inspired reading of the event, but the internal motivation of each person cannot be known in detail.
